title: You’re Defending Truth With a Spirit That Looks Nothing Like the One Who Is Truth.
paragraphs: You’re Defending Truth With a Spirit That Looks Nothing Like the One Who Is Truth.
You may have won the argument, quoted the right verse, exposed the wrong doctrine, and defended biblical truth—and still need to repent for the way you treated the person Jesus told you to love.
There is a frightening possibility nobody likes to consider.
You can be right...
and still be wrong.
Right about the doctrine.
Right about the verse.
Right about the moral issue.
Right about what Scripture actually teaches.
Right about the error you are confronting.
And yet terribly wrong in the spirit with which you confront it.
You can defend the truth while humiliating someone made in the image of God.
You can quote Scripture while enjoying another person's embarrassment.
You can expose falsehood while secretly feeding your pride.
You can call it “boldness” when what you really love is the feeling of winning.
And perhaps the most dangerous moment is when you convince yourself that because your theology is correct, Jesus must automatically approve of everything coming out of your mouth.
He doesn't.
Read that again.
Because some of us have become so concerned with whether our opponent's theology looks like Christ that we have stopped asking whether our own behavior does.

Paul wrote something to Timothy that feels almost painfully relevant in an age of comment sections, reaction videos, theological wars, political hostility, denominational fights, screenshots, subtweets, public shaming, and Christians tearing other Christians apart before an audience of unbelievers.
The Greek text of 2 Timothy 2:24–25 begins:
“δοῦλον δὲ Κυρίου οὐ δεῖ μάχεσθαι...”
Doulon de Kyriou ou dei machesthai...
The sense is striking:
“The Lord's servant must not quarrel.”
Then Paul continues:
“ἀλλὰ ἤπιον εἶναι πρὸς πάντας...”
“But must be gentle toward all...”
Not gentle only toward people who agree with you.
Not gentle only toward Christians from your denomination.
Not gentle only toward people who vote like you.
Not gentle only toward people who speak respectfully first.
Paul says:
“πρὸς πάντας.”
Toward all.
Then comes the phrase that should stop every Christian keyboard warrior for a moment:
“ἐν πραΰτητι παιδεύοντα τοὺς ἀντιδιατιθεμένους...”
En prautēti paideuonta tous antidiatithemenous...
“In gentleness correcting those who oppose...”
Gentleness.
Prautēs.
Not cowardice.
Not doctrinal compromise.
Not pretending lies are truth.
Not refusing to confront sin.
Not smiling politely while souls are being deceived.
Biblical gentleness is strength surrendered to God.
Paul does not tell Timothy to abandon correction.
He tells Timothy how a servant of Jesus corrects.
That distinction matters.
Because Christianity does not require us to choose between truth and love.
Jesus Christ is full of both.
And this is where the mirror gets uncomfortable.
Some of us do not merely want error corrected.
We want the person who said it crushed.
We want applause.
We want screenshots.
We want people underneath our post saying, “You destroyed him.”
We want the satisfaction of watching somebody retreat.
We want to feel intellectually superior.
We want the last word.
And because we attached a Bible verse to the attack, we baptized our flesh and called it discernment.
But listen carefully to Paul's reason for gentleness.
It is breathtaking.
He says correction should happen with gentleness in the hope that:
“μήποτε δώῃ αὐτοῖς ὁ θεὸς μετάνοιαν εἰς ἐπίγνωσιν ἀληθείας...”
Perhaps God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth.
There it is.
Metanoian.
Repentance.
Suddenly the person across from you is no longer merely an opponent to defeat.
They are a soul who needs God.
That changes everything.
Because if repentance is the goal, humiliation cannot be the goal.
If restoration is the goal, destruction cannot be the goal.
If you actually want someone to know Christ more deeply, then their public embarrassment cannot secretly be your entertainment.
And perhaps that is the question we should ask before pressing “Post.”
Do I want this person restored...
or do I want this person destroyed?
Be painfully honest.
Because God already knows.
Maybe you have seen it happen.
A Christian posts something questionable.
Within minutes another believer arrives.
Then another.
Soon nobody is correcting anymore.
They're performing.
Sarcasm gets sharper.
Names are called.
Motives are assigned.
People who have never met the person suddenly know exactly what is supposedly inside their heart.
Somebody digs through ten years of posts.
Somebody makes a meme.
Somebody laughs.
Somebody says, “Cry harder.”
Somebody else says, “I'm just speaking truth.”
And somewhere outside that theological battlefield sits a wounded believer who has been considering returning to church.
Or a skeptic quietly wondering whether Christianity might actually be true.
Or a young Christian trying to understand what following Jesus looks like.
And they watch Christians devour one another while everybody insists they are defending Christ.
Something is wrong with that picture.
Not because truth does not matter.
Truth matters enormously.
Paul himself confronted false teaching. Jesus confronted hypocrisy. The apostles warned the church repeatedly about deception. Scripture never commands believers to become spiritually spineless.
But biblical courage is not cruelty.
Biblical discernment is not contempt.
Biblical correction is not humiliation.
And Christian conviction does not give us permission to forget that the person standing opposite us bears the image of God.
Jesus could speak with astonishing severity.
He overturned tables.
He confronted religious hypocrisy.
He pronounced woes.
He told people uncomfortable truths.
So gentleness cannot mean perpetual softness or avoidance of confrontation.
But look at the Christ we claim to represent.
He touched people others considered unclean.
He ate with people religious society despised.
He spoke with the Samaritan woman whose life was tangled with broken relationships—and He told her the truth without treating her like garbage.
He restored Peter after Peter denied Him.
And while Jesus hung bleeding from a Roman cross, surrounded by mockery and violence, His suffering did not turn Him into the kind of monster His enemies were being toward Him.
That should humble us.
Because sometimes a stranger disagrees with us on Facebook and within three comments we are behaving as though Golgotha never happened.
Jesus said:
“I am the way, and the truth, and the life.”
Truth is not merely a collection of propositions Christians possess.
Truth ultimately has a name.
Jesus Christ.
So if I claim to defend truth while becoming increasingly unlike the One who is Truth, something inside me needs examination.
And maybe that sentence hurts because you already know the conversation.
You remember what you typed.
You remember the person.
You remember that little rush when other Christians liked your response.
You remember reading their wounded reply and feeling...
satisfied.
Nobody else knew.
But you knew.
It stopped being about defending Scripture somewhere along the way.
It became personal.
You wanted them to hurt.
And perhaps you were technically right.
That is what makes this so dangerous.
Being wrong sometimes humbles us.
Being right can intoxicate us.
We start thinking correct doctrine gives us moral permission to behave however we want.
But Scripture does not merely care about what you defend.
Scripture cares about the kind of person you are becoming while defending it.
Paul's command comes in a larger context.

He warns Timothy against foolish controversies that produce quarrels. Then he describes the Lord's servant as gentle toward everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting opponents with gentleness.
Why?
Because God grants repentance.
That destroys spiritual arrogance.
You cannot argue someone into regeneration.
You cannot insult someone into sanctification.
You cannot mock someone into repentance.
You can explain.
You can reason.
You can warn.
You can plead.
You can correct.
You can proclaim.
But only God can open a heart.
That means the Christian enters difficult conversations carrying truth in one hand and humility in the other.
Because you are not the Savior.
Jesus is.
And you were once the person who needed mercy too.
Maybe that is what we forget fastest.
Grace has a terrible way of becoming ordinary to people who have received it for a long time.
We forget what Jesus rescued us from.
We forget the thoughts nobody saw.
The sins nobody discovered.
The pride we disguised.
The lust we hid.
The bitterness we justified.
The lies we told ourselves.
The nights we promised God we would change and then returned to the same chains.
We forget how patient Christ has been with us.
And then somebody else's blindness becomes intolerable.
How quickly forgiven people can become merciless.
But the Gospel leaves no room for superiority at the foot of the cross.
There are no celebrities at Calvary.
No theological champions standing above everyone else.
No righteous people who saved themselves.
There are sinners.
And there is a Savior.
Your salvation was not God's trophy for your intelligence.
It was mercy.
Your understanding of Scripture is not evidence that God should be grateful to have you on His team.
It is grace.
Every truth you understand correctly should make you more grateful, more reverent, more humble—not more intoxicated with yourself.
Yes, defend biblical truth.
Please do.
When Scripture is distorted, speak.
When Christ is misrepresented, speak.
When vulnerable people are being deceived, speak.
When sin is renamed righteousness, speak.
When false teaching enters the church, speak.
Christian gentleness is not silence.
But when you speak, remember whose servant you are.
You are not defending your personal kingdom.
You belong to the crucified King.
There will be moments when truth sounds severe because truth itself confronts us.
There will be boundaries.
There will be rebukes.
There will be occasions when Scripture requires public correction because the error is public and damaging.
There will be times when someone refuses correction.
There will even be times when the most loving thing you can say is an uncompromising “No.”
But cruelty does not become holy simply because the sentence before it was doctrinally accurate.
Contempt is not a fruit of the Spirit.
Arrogance is not spiritual maturity.
Dehumanization is not discernment.
And humiliation is not evangelism.
Perhaps you need to go back tonight.
Back to that comment.
Back to that conversation.
Back to that family member.
Back to that Christian you publicly embarrassed.
Back to the unbeliever you treated as an enemy rather than a person who desperately needs the same Savior you desperately needed.
Maybe the Holy Spirit is not asking you to retract the truth.
Maybe He is asking you to repent of the spirit in which you delivered it.
There is a difference.
You can say:
“What I said about Scripture remains what I believe. But the way I spoke to you was arrogant and unloving. That did not represent Christ faithfully. Please forgive me.”
Do you know how much humility that requires?
Enough to look like Jesus.
And maybe someone reading this has been standing on the other side.
Christians wounded you.
Someone weaponized Scripture against you.
A believer made you feel like a project instead of a person.
Someone publicly humiliated you and then called the humiliation “biblical correction.”
Please hear this carefully.
Their cruelty does not redefine Jesus.
Look at Christ Himself.
Do not measure the Savior solely by people who have represented Him badly.
Come closer to Jesus.
Read His words.
Watch Him move through the Gospels.
Watch holiness encounter brokenness.
Watch truth encounter deception.
Watch righteousness encounter sinners.
And finally...
watch Him walk toward a cross carrying the sins of people who could never rescue themselves.
Including ours.
This is the scandal of grace.
The holy Son of God receives sinners who deserve judgment.
The innocent One bears the penalty of the guilty.
The King wears thorns.
The Creator is mocked by creatures whose lungs continue breathing only because He sustains them.
And He gives Himself.
Not because sin doesn't matter.
Precisely because sin matters so terribly that reconciliation costs blood.
At Calvary, truth and grace do not compete.
They meet.
Sin is so serious that Christ must die.
Grace is so astonishing that Christ willingly does.
And the resurrection announces that sin, death, shame, and the grave do not get the final word.
Jesus does.
That means the Gospel can rewrite the arrogant debater too.
It can rewrite the bitter Christian.
The angry apologist.
The wounded church member.
The keyboard warrior.
The hypocrite.
The skeptic.
The false teacher who repents.
The believer who realizes that somewhere between defending Jesus and defending his ego, he stopped looking like Jesus.
Grace does not merely forgive what we have done.
Grace begins transforming what we are becoming.
So maybe today's repentance is simple.
“Jesus, make me more concerned with representing You faithfully than with winning.”
Maybe it is:
“Jesus, forgive me for enjoying somebody else's humiliation.”
Maybe:
“Jesus, expose every place where I have confused arrogance with courage.”
Or maybe you cannot even form a polished prayer.
Then just tell Him the truth.
He already knows.
Not because typing a comment earns forgiveness.
It doesn't.
Christ alone saves.
But sometimes public honesty breaks the private agreement we have made with our pride.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only believer grieving this.
Not because sharing a post makes anyone more spiritual.
But because your timeline is already discipling somebody.
Every day it teaches people what matters to you.
Imagine interrupting one cycle of Christian outrage with a reminder that conviction and compassion do not have to become enemies.
Imagine one argument ending differently because somebody read this first.
Imagine one believer deleting the cruel comment before posting it.
Imagine one marriage conversation becoming gentler.
One church disagreement becoming more Christlike.
One wounded unbeliever realizing, “Maybe Jesus isn't who angry Christians made me think He was.”
That is worth sharing.
Because the real test will not happen while you are calmly reading these words.
It will happen when someone insults your theology.
When somebody mocks your faith.
When somebody misquotes Scripture with absolute confidence.
When your pulse rises.
When your fingers reach for the keyboard.
When you know exactly how to embarrass them.
That is when you may need to come back and remember:
“The Lord's servant must not quarrel.”
It cannot.
Not because supporting this ministry is a condition for glorifying God.
It isn't.
We glorify God through Christ-centered lives of faith, obedience, worship, love, generosity, truth, and service.
But if this ministry is bearing good fruit in your life, supporting it can be one practical way you choose to help Gospel-centered teaching keep reaching people who need it.
Let Scripture search you.
Because perhaps the greatest danger is not that Christians will stop defending truth.
Perhaps it is that we will defend truth so viciously that people can no longer recognize the One we claim the truth is about.
The world does not need Christians who are ashamed of biblical truth.
And it does not need Christians who use biblical truth as an excuse to become cruel.
It needs men and women so surrendered to Jesus that their courage cannot be purchased by applause, their convictions cannot be bullied into silence, and their hearts cannot be poisoned by hatred.
Strong enough to speak.
Humble enough to listen.
Bold enough to correct.
Gentle enough to remember there is a soul on the other side.
Faithful enough to refuse compromise.
Broken enough to know they still need grace themselves.
Because someday the argument will disappear.
The comments will disappear.
The likes will disappear.
The screenshots will disappear.
The applause will disappear.
And you will stand before the Christ whose name you were defending.
May we discover that we did not become unlike Him while trying to prove that we were right about Him.
You may win the argument and lose the person—but Jesus went to the cross because He came to rescue people, not merely defeat their arguments.
Jesus Christ.
